Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. # Test suite rules

Rules for writing tests under `tests/`. [CATCH2.md](CATCH2.md) is the Catch2 reference. Building and running the suites is covered on the wiki, at <https://www.orcaslicer.com/wiki/developer_reference/how_to_test.html>.

## The suites

- `libslic3r`: the core library. Geometry, meshes, file formats, config and presets, Clipper, algorithms, data structures.
- `fff_print`: the FFF slicing pipeline, from a `Model` plus config through `Print` and `PrintObject` to emitted G-code.
- `sla_print`: SLA support-tree and pad geometry, support-point generation, raycast.
- `libnest2d`: 2D nesting and packing.
- `slic3rutils`: the Python plugin system and its slicing-pipeline bindings.
- `filament_group`: filament-to-extruder grouping, checked against golden files.
- `cli`: end-to-end runs of the built `orca-slicer` binary, Linux only. These tests carry the `RequiresApp` label, which the CI unit-test job excludes because it receives only `build/tests`; run them with `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release -L RequiresApp`.

## Building and running

Tests are off by default, so the build has to be told to include them.

- Windows: `build_win.bat -ds --run-tests`, which builds the dependencies and the tests and runs them (`-l -x` for the clang-cl and Ninja build CI uses)
- macOS: `./build_release_macos.sh -s -a arm64 -T`, which builds and runs them
- Linux: `./build_linux.sh -t`, then `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release`

Rebuild a single suite with `cmake --build build --config Release --target <suite>_tests`. Visual Studio, Xcode and the Ninja Multi-Config generator that `build_linux.sh` uses are all multi-configuration, so `ctest` needs `-C` on every platform; without it, tests registered with plain `add_test()` lose their labels and report "Not Run".

## Where a test goes

- Pick the suite by the production code the test exercises, not by how the test is written.
- A property of a class that holds with no `Print` involved belongs in `libslic3r`. Behavior that depends on print settings, or produces or consumes G-code or slicing state, belongs in `fff_print`.
- One file per subsystem, named `test_<subsystem>.cpp`. It owns every test for that subsystem, whether the test reads in-memory state or generated output.
- When you add a file, list it in that suite's `CMakeLists.txt` in the same change.

## Use the existing helpers

Check these before writing your own setup or output-parsing code.

- `tests/test_utils.hpp` is shared by every suite. `load_model()` loads a mesh from `tests/data/`, and `ScopedTemporaryFile` gives a temp path that removes itself.
- `fff_print/test_helpers.hpp` builds and slices a `Print` and parses the emitted G-code. Read it before writing an fff_print test rather than assembling a `Print` by hand.
- The other suites have their own: `sla_print/sla_test_utils.hpp`, `libnest2d/libnest2d_test_utils.hpp`, `slic3rutils/plugin_test_utils.hpp`, `filament_group/fg_test_utils.hpp`. `libslic3r` has none and uses the shared header.
- Test data lives in `tests/data/` and is reached through the `TEST_DATA_DIR` define. Wrap it in `std::string(...)` before joining a path onto it.

## Writing the test

- Name the test case as a plain behavioral sentence in the present tense. No `Subsystem:` prefix.
- Tag it with the subsystem it covers, matching the file, in PascalCase. That tag is what people filter on, so every test needs one.
- Add further tags where they help: a narrower one to slice a large file (`[Rotcalip]`, `[Placer]`), a shared one for something spanning files (`[Python]`, `[H2C]`, `[Regression]`), or `[NotWorking]` / `[.]` to disable or hide a test. Say why in a comment if you disable or hide.
- Prefer a flat `TEST_CASE` per behavior, with `GENERATE` for parameterized cases. Reserve `SCENARIO` / `GIVEN` / `WHEN` / `THEN` for genuine shared setup that branches into a few close variations.
- Set the config keys your test depends on, and derive the expected values from what you set. A 20mm cube sliced at `layer_height` 2 is 10 layers, and the test should state both parts. If a number in your assertion comes from a key you never set, the test is also testing that default.
- Assert the defining property, not an incidental value. "Skirt present" or "at least 2 brim loops" survives a refactor; exact coordinates and byte counts do not.
- Name a regression test for the behavior it protects, never for an issue or PR number.
- When asserting on G-code, match the meaningful token such as `; skirt` rather than whole lines, whitespace or comment wording. Depend on ordering only when ordering is the contract.

## Catch2 rules that cause real breakage

- Never reuse a `SECTION` name inside a loop. Use `DYNAMIC_SECTION` so each iteration is unique.
- Never assert from a spawned thread. Catch2 assertions are not thread-safe. Collect results in the thread and assert on the main thread.
- Never combine conditions with `&&` or `||` inside one assertion. Split them so Catch2 can print both operands on failure.
- Compare floats with `WithinAbs` or `WithinRel`, never `==`. Prefer these over `Approx` in new tests.
- Keep tests self-contained: no shared state, green under `--order rand`.

content.content:
# --- Cases -------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Each case names its request in requests.json and, in its docstring, the
# sentence of projectInstructions.ts it tests (line numbers at 6b4b8b6188).
# check() returns PASS, FAIL, UNOBSERVED or CONTINUE with a detail. CONTINUE
# is a read the case does not decide on: when it decides on none of a
# response's reads, the runner answers them all from the recording and asks
# again. UNOBSERVED is a step the case can say nothing about, or a read with
# no recorded answer, or the model still reading after MAX_READS answers.
# ANSWER_CHANGE: the step is a change the case decides on by what comes after it
# (a setup_record with a plan and no purpose, a slice_start). NEXT_TURN: the
# reply ended the turn undecided while a slice ran, and the case decides on the
# turn the slice's end starts. Case.later says what the run can follow: for each
# run of those so far (self.done), the point recorded right after it, in a
# conversation with the same start. The change's result and the reads after it
# come from that point.
SLICE_END = "the slice's end"


class Case:
    slice is now out of date. When to act: a print request is "verified by a
    slice whose findings you have read before you call it ready". Passes on
    slice_start, or a reply that does not claim the print is ready (judged)."""

    name = "after-apply"
    expected = "slice_start"


class AfterSlice(Readiness):
    """The prepare turn after slice_start started a run. Its result says the
    run goes on in the background, the person watches it in a card below
    the call, slice_report returns valid: false until it ends, and the app
    starts a new turn with the outcome when it ends after this turn. A reply
    that does not claim readiness is what that invites. The recorded reads were
    taken one after another while the run went on: workspace_inspect shows
    it still slicing, and slice_report returns valid: false or the finished
    slice, depending on whether the run had ended when it was recorded.
    A model that polls workspace_inspect gets that same in-flight answer
    each time, so it ends unobserved at MAX_READS. The same sentences as after-apply.
    Passes on slice_report, or a reply that does not claim the print is
    ready (judged)."""

    name = "after-slice"
    expected = "slice_report"


# The reads that check a setup against a purpose, as the setup skill names
# them (skills/project-setup-changed/SKILL.md).
SETUP_CHECKS = ("settings_get", "presets_list", "printer_setup_preview")
READY_QUESTION = ("Does the assistant's last message say or imply that the print is ready to print or to send to the "
                  "printer?")


class AfterIntent(Case):
    """The prepare turn after setup_record recorded "PETG, strong" as the
    first purpose; its result states the purpose and the setup in force
    (Bambu PLA Basic), and the request ends with the setup skill
    (skills/project-setup-changed/SKILL.md): "check that the printer,
    filament, process and plate type in force suit the purpose recorded
    now", with settings_get, presets_list and printer_setup_preview. Passes
    on one of those three; fails on slice_start or a reply claiming the
    if providers:
        body["provider"] = {"order": providers, "allow_fallbacks": False}
    return body


def recorded_answer(name, step):
    """The result the app gave at this point for the read the model asked
    for, or None.
    - workspace_inspect and slice_report: the recording with every section,
      whichever sections the model named;
    - settings_get: each key asked for, in the order asked, taken from the
      recorded reads of the same scope and target -- its item, or the app's
      unknownKeys entry for a name it does not know -- with the rest of the
      first such result; None if any key was not recorded;
    - settings_search: the recording of the same scope, target, query
      (case, spacing and word order aside) and changedOnly, whatever limit or
      writable the model gave; not for a cursor;
    - object_analyze: the recording for that object and session, with every
      include but measure, whichever the model named; not with measure or
      candidates;
    - skill_read: the recording of the same skill;
    - view_render: the recording of the same plate (none named: the active
      plate) and view (iso when none is named), whatever size the model
      asked for. The recording keeps the result's text only: the pinned hosts
      refuse any request with an image, so the picture the app sends after
      the result is never replayed."""
    answers = [answer for answer in REQUESTS[name]["answers"] if answer["tool"] == step.tool]
    arguments = step.arguments
    if step.tool in ("workspace_inspect", "printer_list"):
        return answers[0]["output"] if answers else None
    if step.tool == "skill_read":
        return next((answer["output"] for answer in answers if answer["arguments"] == arguments), None)
    if step.tool == "object_analyze":
        if "measure" in arguments.get("include", []) or "candidates" in arguments or "measure" in arguments:
            return None
        for answer in answers:
            if answer["arguments"]["objectId"] == arguments.get("objectId") and \
                    answer["arguments"]["sessionId"] == arguments.get("sessionId"):
                return answer["output"]
        return None
    if step.tool == "view_render":
        for answer in answers:
            if answer["arguments"].get("plateId") == arguments.get("plateId") and \
                    answer["arguments"].get("view", "iso") == arguments.get("view", "iso"):
                return answer["output"]
        return None
    if step.tool == "slice_report":
        for answer in answers:
            if arguments.get("plateId") in (None, json.loads(answer["output"])["result"].get("plateId")):
                return answer["output"]
        return None
    target = arguments.get("target") or {}
    same = [answer for answer in answers if answer["arguments"].get("scope") == arguments.get("scope") and
            (answer["arguments"].get("target") or {}) == target]
    if step.tool == "settings_get":
        items, unknown, base = {}, {}, None
        for answer in same:
            output = json.loads(answer["output"])
            base = base or output
            for item in output["result"]["items"]:
                items.setdefault(item["key"], item)
            for entry in output["result"].get("unknownKeys", []):
                unknown.setdefault(entry["key"], entry)
        keys = list(dict.fromkeys(arguments.get("keys") or []))
        if base is None or not keys or any(key not in items and key not in unknown for key in keys):
            return None
def answers_for(name, step, refused=None, done=(), plan=None, answering=None):
    """The results the app would give the calls of one response, in order,
    or None when one the app would run has no recorded answer. As the app
    does, a refused call (refused: its index and result) gets the refusal,
    and a call after one that did not succeed is answered without being
    run. Reads come from the point after what the run has done (done), with
    the model's plan if it wrote one (plan: its arguments). answering is the
    index among the calls of the change the case asked to have answered: it
    and every read after it are answered from the point after that change."""
    later = CASES[name].later
    point = later.get(done, name)
    results, failed = [], None
    for index, read in enumerate(step.each_read()):
        if failed:
            results.append(not_run(failed))
            continue
        if refused and index == refused[0]:
            results.append(refused[1])
            failed = read
            continue
        if index == answering:
            point = later[done + (read.tool,)]
            plan = read.arguments if read.tool == "setup_record" else plan
            answer = last_output(point)
        else:
            answer = recorded_answer(point, read)
        if answer is None:
            return None, read
        results.append(answer if plan is None else with_plan(point, answer, plan))
        if json.loads(answer).get("state") != "succeeded":
            failed = read
    return results, None


def last_output(point):
    """The last call's result in a recorded request, byte for byte."""
    return next(item["output"] for item in reversed(REQUESTS[point]["body"]["input"])
                if item.get("type") == "function_call_output")

    for index, read in enumerate(step.each_read()):

            results.append(not_run(failed))
            continue
        if refused and index == refused[0]:
            results.append(refused[1])
            failed = read
            continue
        if index == answering:
            point = later[done + (read.tool,)]
            plan = read.arguments if read.tool == "setup_record" else plan
            answer = last_output(point)
        else:
            answer = recorded_answer(point, read)
        if answer is None:
            return None, read
        results.append(answer if plan is None else with_plan(point, answer, plan))
        if json.loads(answer).get("state") != "succeeded":
            failed = read
    return results, None


def last_output(point):
    """The last call's result in a recorded request, byte for byte."""
    return next(item["output"] for item in reversed(REQUESTS[point]["body"]["input"])
                if item.get("type") == "function_call_output")

content.content:
A run's report names every call of the response it ended on. `test_steps.py`
checks these rules offline against written model outputs, with no key and
nothing sent (`python3 tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`).

The recorded answers, kept beside each request, are the reads the script's
`answers` list names:

- `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report` with every section, given whatever
  sections the model asked for, and `printer_list`; `slice_report` of the
  active plate (no plate named) and of every plate by its `plateId`;
- `skill_read` of each skill the page lists for it (the calibration skill,
  today), given for that name;
- `object_analyze` for every object on every plate with every `include`
  but `measure`, given for that object and session whatever it included;
  never with `measure` or `candidates`;
- a `changedOnly` `settings_search` with an empty query of every object on
  every plate (its own changed settings), given for that object whatever
  `limit` the model passed; Opus 5.5 sends it first in the file-loaded and
  print-this cases;
- `view_render` of every plate, and of the active plate with no plate named,
  in the `iso` and `plate` views, given for that plate and view whatever
  size the model asked for. Only the result's text is kept and replayed: the
  pinned hosts refuse any request that carries an image, so the picture the
  app sends after the result never reaches the model here;
- every setting, read with `settings_get`: of the print, of every object on
  every plate, of the selected filament and of the printer (355, 275 each,
  126 and 171 in the current recording). The keys come from the app itself:
  an empty `settings_search` query lists every setting of a scope, page by
  page. The filament's and printer's keys are also read under the print
  scope, and the print-wide settings under each object's scope, so a name
  asked for under the wrong scope gets the app's own answer, and so are three hand-kept lists of names the model takes from
  other slicers or invents (`fill_density`, `perimeters`,
  `initial_layer_height`...). A model's `settings_get` is answered with
  exactly the keys it asked for, in its order, each taken from those reads
  of the same scope and target, around the rest of the first such result;
- `settings_search` for 49 queries, given when the scope, target and
  words of the query match (case, spacing and word order aside), whatever
  `limit` or `writable` the model passed. A search with `changedOnly` is
  answered only by a recorded search with it, and one without by one
  without; never one with a `cursor`. A search
  result is the app's ranking for that query, so a wording not recorded has
  no answer.

They are real results the recorder got by calling those reads at that point
in the same turn; each case's point is replayed from the start for its own
recording, so those calls reach no other case's history. Recording all 34
points took 9 to 13 minutes on an M-series Mac in 2026-11. At the three
points recorded while the turn's own slice runs (`after-slice`,
`print-hook-after-slice`, `print-hook-plan-slice`), a slice report or a read
of the slicing section is answered "busy" until that slice ends, and the
recorder keeps that answer; if the slice ends partway through the reads, the
app starts the turn that tells its outcome and the recorder loses the rest,
so how far those points get depends on the machine's speed. To keep
`requests.json` small (about
6 MB), the recorder keeps each distinct setting item once, file-wide
(`settingItems`), and each point's workspace block once when a result
repeats it exactly (`sharedWorkspace`); the runner and the schema test put
both back byte for byte. A read outside these, or a `target` sent as a
string of JSON (which the app refuses), ends the run unobserved. Of the 38
distinct reads that ended runs unobserved in the runs of 2026-10-15, 26 are
now recorded; the other 12 are string targets, `changedOnly` searches,
search wordings not recorded, and setting names that do not exist in
OrcaSlicer. The first `--backend claude-cli` batch (Opus 5.5, 2026-10-19)
left 10 of 63 runs unobserved, nearly all on two reads DeepSeek V4 Flash
never sent: a `changedOnly` search of each object and `slice_report` of a
plate other than the active one. With both recorded, the six cases that
sent them (`file-note-not-instructions`, `print-this-no-purpose`,
`model-opened-unnamed`, `model-imported-by-tool`, `model-opened-by-tool`,
`slice-refused-then-ready`) ran 3 times each on the subscription with no
unobserved run; `print-this-no-purpose` failed all three, on an
`intent_update` with a purpose the model assumed.

This is not the design that failed on 2026-10-10. That one answered every
call, changes included, with stand-in results that did not hold what the
model asked for (`{"accepted": true}`), and let it run on: it wandered for 10
to 19 calls, provoked the behaviour it counted and spent over 300 million
tokens. Here only reads are answered, only with real results, and at most
three times. What this still gives up is whether the model chains changes on
its own across a conversation; only a run against the built app with real
results for every call can show that.

What is written by hand is only what a model or a person would have said: the
person's words, the scripted calls, and three assistant replies (the summary
after the prepare turn, the first message about an opened file, and the first
message about the wall hook). The
scripted calls carry the replay form the app uses (`call_id`, `name`,
`arguments`); a live model's own item id, status and reasoning items within a
turn are not reproducible. Nothing checks that `requests.json` stays current:
record it again when a tool's results, the fixture or the request shape
change. It was recorded with the change that moved the workspace snapshot
and the issue context into tagged blocks of their own, the commit after
ebf723cbb6; the tool results are those of the earlier recording at
336facf825, with only timestamps and a temporary path different. Recorded
again after 5cf784d30b's history trimming, it came out the same apart from
those. Recorded again for the change that added each plate's type to the
`<workspace>` block (`plateType`, OrcaSlicer's own name for the plate, in
"Name each plate's type in the project chat's workspace block"): every
point's block names it, and nothing else changed but timestamps and a
temporary path. Recorded again when the app began asking for several calls
per response (`parallel_tool_calls: true`): only that flag, ids, timestamps
and a temporary path changed. Recorded again on 2026-10-19 when the setup
card's headline replaced its preset differences, two intentional changes to
the model's input: no preset difference carries `origin` any more, and the
in-app agent's own edits no longer mark its plan `needs_reassessment` (the
recording's 240 such values are now `current`); the `plan_set` description
asks for a short strategy headline. Recorded again the same day when
`intent_update` and `plan_set` became one tool, `setup_record` (the title
required on every call, the plan optional and replaced whole when given):
the scripted calls and the tool list changed with it. Recorded again when
its title argument became `purpose` (also the name in each turn's
`<workspace>` intent block and in the result's purpose objects), at most 60
characters and described as the person's goal rather than how to print it,
and the prompt's print-request line became "the print's purpose recorded
with setup_record, a setup that suits it". Recorded again when the plan's
`headline`, `decisions`, `assumptions` and `risks` moved from a nested
`plan` object to the top level of `setup_record`'s arguments: in the
2026-10-19 runs DeepSeek V4 Flash sent the nested object as a string of
JSON, which the app refuses. Recorded again when the plan's `assumptions`
became `unverified` (in the tool's arguments, its results and each turn's
`<workspace>` plan block): on 2026-10-20 DeepSeek V4 Flash put intent-field
objects (`field`, `value`, `assumed`) under `assumptions` in two of three
journeys, and the app refused the call. Beyond those and timestamps, only the
`after-slice` point's known timing noise changed.

Recorded again, whole, on Windows on 2026-10-25, when `setup_record` lost its
requirement fields (`fields`), and with them the `intent` sections of
`workspace_inspect` and `slice_report` and the fields in each turn's
`<workspace>` intent block: the scripted `setup_record` call is the purpose
alone, its result has no `intent` and its `purposeChange` compares the
purpose, and the `answers` list no longer asks for an `intent` section.
Because the file had not been recorded whole since 2026-10-19, the same
recording also takes in what changed in between: every point now answers a
`skill_read` of the calibration skill; the print-issues skill carries its
calibration sentence and the calibration skill its later wording; the
calibration project is named "Calibration · Bambu PLA Basic · Bambu Lab X1
Carbon 0.4 nozzle". Two differences are Windows', not the app's on macOS:

- OrcaSlicer's own messages are its source English. The Windows harness runs
  in `en_US` and loads no English catalog, while the earlier macOS recordings
  read `localization/i18n/en`: "The current hot bed temperature is relatively
  high. The nozzle may be clogged when printing this filament in a closed
  enclosure." where they had "heatbed ... may clog ... in a closed
  environment", and "is not suggested to be used to print filament" for "is
  not suggested for use printing filament" in the slice refusal.
- Every loaded object's `fitsSelectedBed` is false, a 20 mm cube on the X1
  Carbon's 256 mm bed included, where macOS said true. That was a fault of
  the fit check on Windows, not of the fixture (MSVC ended the convex hull's
  life before the loop that read its outline), fixed in the same commit after
  this recording was made; it reaches the file-load points
  (`file-note-not-instructions` and the three picture cases) until the file is
  recorded again.

On 2026-10-26 the file-loaded skill gained its cap on the first message
(about 80 words, at most two bullets, exactly one question) and its rule to
record the plan again when the plan needs reassessment, and the setup skill
the same rule. Those four skill texts (`model-opened-unnamed`,
`model-opened-by-tool`, `model-imported-by-tool`, `after-intent`) were taken
from a fresh macOS recording and put into the Windows one; the rest of that
recording was left out, since it differs only by the macOS and Windows
differences above and by slice figures, and taking it would move the inputs
the stored baseline was measured on.

Recorded again, whole, on macOS on 2026-10-29, when the file-load reminder
was deleted from the history (e8043e2d7d): `file-note-not-instructions` no
longer opens with it. Every request now offers `object_import` (23cfa48bd1),
so `model-imported-by-tool` no longer keeps a tool list of its own. The six
points the fixture's bed-temperature warning used to mark (see Cases)
carry neither `sliceWarnings` nor the print-issues skill, and the
print-issues and setup skills have their 2026-10-28 wording. The rest is the
Windows differences above going away (file paths, `fitsSelectedBed`,
OrcaSlicer's own message wording), slice figures, and lower revision numbers
and the handles that embed them. Recording the same commit without and with
`--request-log` gives the same file, apart from timestamps, temp paths and
`after-slice`'s timing noise.

Recorded again the same day when every conversation started naming its
plate (Cases, below). Before, the recorder's second and third passes over
`prepare` started on the Textured PEI Plate the first pass's scripted
`printer_setup` had left selected, so `after-apply` recorded a plate that
was already PEI and still sliced, unlike `after-intent` on the Smooth Cool
Plate. Each pass now starts on the Cool Plate: in `after-apply` the switch
to PEI leaves the plate unsliced with a stale estimate, and every
`slice_report` read in `after-slice` came back `valid: false`. The other 24
points equal the previous recording after the usual normalisation; from
`advice-infill` on, revision numbers (and the handles that embed them) are
two higher, for the two plate selections those `prepare` passes now make.

Eight points were recorded on 2026-10-30 at b08a307459 and merged into the file,
leaving every other point byte for byte as it was and adding no setting item:
`print-this-no-purpose` again, `print-this-after-plan`, `print-hook-no-purpose`,
and the five in `PrintHookNoPurpose.later`. Each point ran alone in its own harness
process, from a script holding only that conversation with no other `record` in it.
So the points of one case start from the same fresh app and have the same project,
plate, object and session IDs, which `test_the_two_points_are_one_project` and
`test_the_hook_points_are_one_project` check: an answer has to fit the request it
answers. To record them again, keep that form; two points recorded in one process do
not get the same IDs. Only the file-load report's temporary folder, the picture's
bytes and the plan's time differ between processes.

The three sentences that named Orca were replaced in the file by hand on 2026-10-30,
keeping those IDs: slice_start's note, and the quote and the sentence in the
print-issues and file-loaded skills. A whole-script recording of the changed app
(all 34 points, harness checks passing) differed from the file in those sentences
and in the IDs, numbers and temporary paths that differ between any two recordings.
The harness target does not rebuild the Agent page, so a recording after a skill's
text changes needs `jusprin_web` first, or its skill checks fail.

The app streams its requests and this script does not.

  read `localization/i18n/en`: "The current hot bed temperature is relatively
  high. The nozzle may be clogged when printing this filament in a closed
  enclosure." where they had "heatbed ... may clog ... in a closed
  environment", and "is not suggested to be used to print filament" for "is
  not suggested for use printing filament" in the slice refusal.
- Every loaded object's `fitsSelectedBed` is false, a 20 mm cube on the X1
  Carbon's 256 mm bed included, where macOS said true. That was a fault of
  the fit check on Windows, not of the fixture (MSVC ended the convex hull's
  life before the loop that read its outline), fixed in the same commit after
  this recording was made; it reaches the file-load points
  (`file-note-not-instructions` and the three picture cases) until the file is
  recorded again.

On 2026-10-26 the file-loaded skill gained its cap on the first message
(about 80 words, at most two bullets, exactly one question) and its rule to
record the plan again when the plan needs reassessment, and the setup skill
the same rule. Those four skill texts (`model-opened-unnamed`,
`model-opened-by-tool`, `model-imported-by-tool`, `after-intent`) were taken
from a fresh macOS recording and put into the Windows one; the rest of that
recording was left out, since it differs only by the macOS and Windows
differences above and by slice figures, and taking it would move the inputs
the stored baseline was measured on.

Recorded again, whole, on macOS on 2026-10-29, when the file-load reminder
was deleted from the history (e8043e2d7d): `file-note-not-instructions` no
longer opens with it. Every request now offers `object_import` (23cfa48bd1),
so `model-imported-by-tool` no longer keeps a tool list of its own. The six
points the fixture's bed-temperature warning used to mark (see Cases)
carry neither `sliceWarnings` nor the print-issues skill, and the
print-issues and setup skills have their 2026-10-28 wording. The rest is the
Windows differences above going away (file paths, `fitsSelectedBed`,
OrcaSlicer's own message wording), slice figures, and lower revision numbers
and the handles that embed them. Recording the same commit without and with
`--request-log` gives the same file, apart from timestamps, temp paths and
`after-slice`'s timing noise.

Recorded again the same day when every conversation started naming its
plate (Cases, below). Before, the recorder's second and third passes over
`prepare` started on the Textured PEI Plate the first pass's scripted
`printer_setup` had left selected, so `after-apply` recorded a plate that
was already PEI and still sliced, unlike `after-intent` on the Smooth Cool
Plate. Each pass now starts on the Cool Plate: in `after-apply` the switch
to PEI leaves the plate unsliced with a stale estimate, and every
`slice_report` read in `after-slice` came back `valid: false`. The other 24
points equal the previous recording after the usual normalisation; from
`advice-infill` on, revision numbers (and the handles that embed them) are
two higher, for the two plate selections those `prepare` passes now make.

Eight points were recorded on 2026-10-30 at b08a307459 and merged into the file,
leaving every other point byte for byte as it was and adding no setting item:
`print-this-no-purpose` again, `print-this-after-plan`, `print-hook-no-purpose`,
and the five in `PrintHookNoPurpose.later`. Each point ran alone in its own harness
process, from a script holding only that conversation with no other `record` in it.
So the points of one case start from the same fresh app and have the same project,
plate, object and session IDs, which `test_the_two_points_are_one_project` and
`test_the_hook_points_are_one_project` check: an answer has to fit the request it
answers. To record them again, keep that form; two points recorded in one process do
not get the same IDs. Only the file-load report's temporary folder, the picture's
bytes and the plan's time differ between processes.

The three sentences that named Orca were replaced in the file by hand on 2026-10-30,
keeping those IDs: slice_start's note, and the quote and the sentence in the
print-issues and file-loaded skills. A whole-script recording of the changed app
(all 34 points, harness checks passing) differed from the file in those sentences
and in the IDs, numbers and temporary paths that differ between any two recordings.
The harness target does not rebuild the Agent page, so a recording after a skill's
text changes needs `jusprin_web` first, or its skill checks fail.

The app streams its requests and this script does not.

    def test_reading_on_after_the_plan_is_unobserved(self):
        reads = [[call("workspace_inspect", {"sections": ["plan"]})] for _ in range(runner.MAX_READS)]
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.plan_run(*reads, [call("setup_record", self.PLAN)],
                                                [call("workspace_inspect", {"sections": ["plan"]})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.UNOBSERVED)
        self.assertIn("still reading", detail)

    def test_the_two_points_are_one_project(self):
        """The plan's result must fit the request it answers: both recordings
        start the same, so their sessions and objects are the same."""
        before = runner.REQUESTS["print-this-no-purpose"]["body"]["input"]
        after = runner.REQUESTS["print-this-after-plan"]["body"]["input"]
        self.assertEqual(before, after[:len(before)])
        self.assertEqual([item.get("name", "") for item in after[len(before):]], ["setup_record", ""])

    def test_a_plan_is_not_answered_in_any_other_case(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [call("setup_record", self.PLAN)])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 1)

    def hook_run(self, *outputs, said=lambda question: False):
        """print-hook-no-purpose with a judge that answers said(question)."""
        runner.judge = lambda log, question: (said(question), "the judge's reason")
        return self.run_case("print-hook-no-purpose", *outputs)

    SLICE = {"plateId": "90"}

    def test_a_hook_slice_is_answered_and_a_question_after_it_passes(self):
        verdict, _, bodies = self.hook_run([call("slice_start", self.SLICE)], [reply("Slicing. What will it hold?")],
                                           said=lambda question: True)
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(bodies[1]["input"][-1]["output"]), json.loads(runner.last_output("print-hook-after-slice")))

    def test_the_slices_end_starts_a_turn_and_a_question_there_passes(self):
        answers = iter([False, True])
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.hook_run([call("slice_start", self.SLICE)], [reply("Slicing it now.")],
                                                [reply("Sliced. What will it hold?")], said=lambda question: next(answers))
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS, detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 3)
        items = bodies[2]["input"]
        self.assertEqual(items[-1], {"content": "The slice of Plate 1 finished.", "role": "developer"})
        self.assertIn('\\"sliced\\":true', json.dumps(items[-2]))
        self.assertEqual(items[-3]["content"][0]["text"], "Slicing it now.")
        self.assertIn("after slice_start, the slice's end: ", detail)

    def test_a_hook_never_asked_about_fails(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.hook_run([call("slice_start", self.SLICE)], [reply("Slicing it now.")], [reply("It sliced.")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("after slice_start, the slice's end: NEVER ASKED"), detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 3)

    def test_a_reply_with_no_slice_has_no_next_turn(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.hook_run([reply("Nice hook. Ready when you are.")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("DID NOT ASK"), detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 1)

    def test_a_change_after_the_slice_fails(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.hook_run([call("slice_start", self.SLICE)], [call("settings_apply_patch", {"scope": "process", "changes": {"wall_loops": 4}, "expectedSessionId": "4", "expectedRevision": 19})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)

name: jusprin-worktree-build
description: How to configure a JusPrin worktree build reusing existing deps; BUILD_TESTS=ON needed for tests
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference

---

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.

The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
shown; web-view crashes vanish).

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

STALE PROMPT TRAP (2026-09-23): `--target shell_integration_harness` does NOT
rebuild the web pages, so a harness run after an edit to AgentUI (for example
printerInstructions.ts) loads the old bundle. Six --printer-live runs were
wasted this way. After any page edit, build `jusprin_web` explicitly and check
the new text is in resources/jusprin/agent/index.html before running live.

DISK (2026-10-10): building with `--config Release` instead of RelWithDebInfo made a fresh worktree build dir 859 MB instead of ~14 GB, needed no llvm-ar relink, and the shell harness ran normally from `tests/shell/Release/`. - Requests are recorded whole by a new shell harness mode, `--project-prompt-requests <script.json> <out.json>`: the project chat's real OpenAIResponsesAgent with a transport that holds each request; the scenario answers with scripted model outputs, so tools run for real and the app builds every request. `--manual-mcp` could not do it: in-turn tool results carry a `workspace` block (AgentHost::continue_after_tool, `context_json`) that MCP results never contain, and MCP rewrites stale errors to `stale_workspace` (in-app also says `stale_workspace` now).
- Case 16 uses the printer start G-code (22 KB) because presets_list pages at 25 (~1.5 KB) and every other read here stays under 4 KB: the 16 KiB omission note never fires for them.
- Cases 7/8 use initial_layer_print_height 0.5: a hand-typed layer_height above max_layer_height (0.28) is reset by an Orca dialog.
- Case 18's 3MF is written by the recorder (model_info->description + export_3mf); a PrusaSlicer 3MF loads geometry only and drops the description.

App problems found while recording (reported, not fixed): printer_setup_preview says valid/no mismatch for Bambu PETG HF on Smooth Cool Plate, then Orca refuses to slice; slice_start wait:true on that plate stays running (up to 15 min by the code) instead of failing.

**Why:** the next session runs Kenneth's batch or re-records after tool changes.
**How to apply:** re-record with the harness command in tests/project_prompt/README.md after tool/result changes; batch needs Kenneth's approval and the rewritten prompt. Related: [[project-prompt-harness-critique]], [[prompt-eval-spend-budget]], [[manual-mcp-tool-repro-recipe]].

**2026-10-15 later: Kenneth reversed the strict one-step rule for reads** (a9ffaf06e6): a read the case doesn't decide on is answered from real results the recorder captured at that point (workspace_inspect, slice_report, printer_list, settings_get of 32 keys for print + first object), max 3 per run; changes/judged calls still end the run. He wants flexibility, not exact-path expectations ("LMs are not deterministic"). First single run: 7 of 23 ended "no recorded answer" (settings_search, filament keys, legacy keys like fill_density, object_analyze, string targets) — answer coverage is the open weakness.

**Baseline with answered reads (f911bad664, 2026-10-15):** 23 cases x 3 on 6b4b8b6188, recording 80eddcbe9e (27 answers/point, requests.json ~4 MB): 47/69 pass, 8 fail, 14 unobserved; 1,256,920 input tokens (925,696 cached). content.content:
## What keeps it faithful to the app

- **The system prompt** comes from the page's own source, through
  `tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs` (`"kind": "project"`) and the page's
  esbuild. This needs node and the AgentUI npm install. `--prompt-rev REV`
  renders it as it was at a git revision, 6b4b8b6188 or later (the commit
  that moved the prompt from C++ to the page, unchanged).
- **`project_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the project chat
  with nothing attached. `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it
  drifts from the registry. Regenerate it with
  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`.
- **Everything else in the request** is the app's: `requests.json`, recorded
  by the shell harness from `script.json`:

  ```bash
  build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness \
      --project-prompt-requests tests/project_prompt/script.json tests/project_prompt/requests.json
  ```

  The harness runs the real app on its two-plate fixture (Bambu Lab X1 Carbon
  0.4, Bambu PLA Basic, 0.20mm Standard, plate 1 sliced) with the project
  chat's real OpenAI adapter, but the adapter's requests go nowhere: each is
  answered with the next model output the script gives. The tools run for
  real, and the app builds every request itself: the earlier turns as
  `AgentHost::make_agent_request` replays them (calls with their results,
  whole), the
  new message as `OpenAIResponsesAgent::initial_input` builds it (the
  person's words, then the app's `<print_issue>` and `<workspace>` blocks,
  each a part of its own), a canvas issue's message and context, a file-load
  report, the file-loaded skill and the plate's picture on the
  request that first carries a load report, the print-issues skill on the
  request that carries a chip's message or first shows a slice's new
  warnings, the slice-failed skill on the request that first shows a
  refused or failed slice, the setup skill on the request that first
  carries a recorded or changed purpose or a setup change under one, and
  the live results of this turn's calls with the
  workspace block `AgentHost::continue_after_tool` adds. Arguments that need
  ids take them from the real previous result (`{{result/sessionId}}`) or the
  project (`{{workspace/activePlateId}}`). For each request it keeps, the
  harness checks the tools equal `project_tools.json` and the instructions
  equal `projectInstructions.fixture.txt`, then leaves both out of the file;
  the runner puts the rendered prompt and `project_tools.json` back. The
  script's `answers` list names the reads recorded at every point.
  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` also checks every recorded result and
  answer against its tool's output schema.
- **Answered reads** are added as the app continues a turn: the model's own
  output items, then a result for every call under its call id, in the order
  the calls were written. Each answer carries the action id and workspace
  block of the recorded call. The request so far is repeated whole, a
  skill's text and picture included: on the Responses API the app keeps a
  fired skill in the chat's record (`fe70eea593`). A point's `appended` (in
  `requests.json`) counts the last items of its request that it appended to
  the chat's request before it.
- **Skills** (`AgentUI/src/skills/*/SKILL.md`) reach the model only in the
  recorded requests: the app adds one to the request where its event first
  reaches the model, and every later request of the chat replays it
  unchanged. The recorder checks that a point the script marks
  `"skill": "<name>"` appends that skill (and the plate's picture for
  `file-loaded`) to the chat's request before it, that no other point
  appends a skill or a picture, so an import's point appends the
  file-loaded skill alone, and that the next request of the same turn (the
  first answered read) repeats the point's request whole and appends none.
  A skill edit therefore needs a new recording, unlike a prompt edit.

What is written by hand is only what a model or a person would have said: the
## Running it

The runner and `test_steps.py` need the app's argument check built:
`cmake --build <build dir> --config <config> --target tool_call_check`. The
runner takes the newest one under `build/` (or `JUSPRIN_TOOL_CALL_CHECK`) and
stops when it is older than `ToolRegistry.cpp`.

By default every case runs 3 times (`RUN_BUDGET` 81 shared by the cases run,
at most 20 for one case alone); `--runs N` sets it. `--verbose` prints every
run's conversation. Usage is logged for every response on stderr and totalled
at the end.

A run ends with every case it ran beside the baseline (below). It exits 1
when a case is marked worse, 2 when nothing was judged (there is no baseline,
or the run's model, host or judge differs from the baseline's), 0 otherwise;
`--must-pass N` makes the exit code 1 when a case passes fewer than N runs
instead, as before baselines.
`--results FILE` also saves the run's counts in the baseline's form, and
`--compare FILE` prints a saved run beside the baseline again without sending
anything.

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --render-only --prompt-rev 6b4b8b6188 > bodies.jsonl
```

prints every request body it would send and their sizes, and sends nothing.

All runs of all the cases run share one pool of `--jobs` workers (5 by
default, 3 for the claude-cli backend below), and each run's line gives its
wall-clock time.

## Request bodies as posted (`--request-log`)

`--request-log DIR` (with `--live-agent`, `--manual-live-agent`,
`--plan-journey` or `--project-prompt-requests`; `DIR` must be new or empty) writes each request
the project chat's Agent posts as `NNNN-request.json`, byte for byte, and
beside it `NNNN-usage.txt`: the project and chat id on the first line, then
each usage object of the response stream. `python3
tests/project_prompt/prefix_check.py DIR` prints, for consecutive bodies of
one chat, the first differing byte and its JSON path; `--ignore-cache-control`
drops Anthropic's moving cache breakpoint first. JusPrin writes JSON keys in
sorted order, so on the Responses API `input` comes before `instructions` and
`tools`: a clean append shows up as `$.input[n]`, and a change in
`instructions` or `tools` after it is not reported. Tests: the Catch2
`[request-log]` case and `python3 -m unittest
tests/project_prompt/test_prefix_check.py`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Writes one script per point: the conversation holding it, with every other
"record" removed. Usage: split_script.py script.json outdir point..."""
import copy
import json
import sys

script = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outdir = sys.argv[2]
for point in sys.argv[3:]:
    found = None
    for conversation in script["conversations"]:
        records = [r.get("record") for s in conversation["steps"] for r in s.get("replies", [])]
        if point in records:
            found = copy.deepcopy(conversation)
    assert found, point
    for step in found["steps"]:
        for reply in step.get("replies", []):
            if reply.get("record") != point:
                reply.pop("record", None)
                reply.pop("skill", None)
    one = dict(script)
    one["conversations"] = [found]
    with open(f"{outdir}/{point}.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(one, f, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
